module.title: Breast Cancer Screening
module.intro: In this module, you will learn about various methods of screening for breast cancer.

slides.title: Why do we screen for breast cancer?

items: Screening refers to tests used to find breast cancer in people who don't have symptoms
Breast cancer screening uses imaging tests like mammograms, ultrasounds and MRI to look for cancer at an early stage
Finding cancer early means it is smaller and easier to treat
This is why regular breast cancer screening is so important

blocks.text: Think of it like a smoke detector that warns you about an early fire!

media.alt: Illustration of a ceiling smoke detector with alarm signals radiating from it.

slides.title: Benefits and Potential Harms of Screening

items.title: Finding cancer early
items.text: Screening can detect breast cancer before a lump can be felt or symptoms develop.

items.title: Less treatment
items.text: When cancer is found early, it is often smaller and easier to treat. This may allow for less extensive surgery and fewer treatments.

items.title: Better outcomes
items.text: Early detection can lower risk of dying from cancer.

items.title: False positives
items.text: A false positive is when a screening test shows something that looks like cancer, but turns out not to be cancer. Think of it like a broken fire alarm that goes off when there is no fire.

items.title: Extra tests
items.text: If something unusual appears on a screening test, your doctor may recommend more imaging or a biopsy. These tests often show no cancer, but the process can cause worry and discomfort.

blocks.text: A false positive is when a screening test flags an abnormality that needs further workup but turns out not to be cancer.
Think of it like a fire alarm when there is no fire!

items.text: For women who got MRIs, 10 out of 100 patients will need further testing and most of those will be benign. These are false positives.
Extra tests can lead to more worry, cost, discomfort. The benefits often outweigh the risks

items: Mammograms use a small amount of radiation, but the risk of radiation-related cancer is very low.
For most women, the benefits of screening outweigh this risk of radiation exposure.
The main purpose of screening is to detect breast cancer early.
Screening can detect cancer before symptoms develop.
The benefits of screening (early detection, less treatment, better outcomes) need to be weighed against the harms (false positive results, biopsies, over diagnosis).

For many people mammograms are uncomfortable rather than truly painful.

items.a: Breast ultrasound uses sound waves to make images of the breast.

items.q: When do you get a breast ultrasound?
items.a: Often used for screening in addition to mammography or as a follow-up test after an abnormal finding on a screening mammogram, MRI, or breast exam

blocks.heading: What to expect:
items: Undress from waist up
Lie on exam table
Cold jelly applied to breast
Ultrasound technologist will move probe over breast

media.alt: Photograph of a gloved hand moving an ultrasound probe over a patient's chest, with the ultrasound screen behind.

items.a: Breast MRI uses magnetic fields to create an image of the breast

items.q: When do you get a breast MRI?
items.a: Breast MRI is used for breast cancer screening for women at high risk and with dense breasts

blocks.heading: Why doesn't everyone get an MRI?
items: Requires contrast dye injected into your vein (through an IV) which some people may have allergies to
More likely than a mammogram to have false positive results
The machine can feel loud, narrow, or uncomfortable for some people
May not always be covered by insurance
Cannot be performed if pregnant or if you have certain types of metal in your body

media.alt: Medical diagram of a patient lying face down on a table that slides into the bore of an MRI machine.

Change into gown
IV placed in arm to give contrast

items.title: Positioning

items: Lie on your stomach
Breasts rest in cushioned openings
A safety button is provided to press if needed

items.title: Imaging
items.alt: Photograph of an MRI table sliding a patient into the machine.
items: Table slides into MRI machine
Contrast is given
You will hear loud tapping noises

blocks.text: Most mammography centers use the Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS®) to classify findings in a standard way. You may see this on a radiology report.

rows.meaning: Short-term follow-up imaging in 6 months recommended
Biopsy recommended to know if benign or cancerous

items.a: A breast biopsy uses a needle to take a sample of breast tissue to check for cancer. It is the only test that can confirm whether something is cancer.

items.q: Why do you get a breast biopsy?
items.a: If a lump, breast change, or imaging test (like a mammogram or ultrasound) looks abnormal, your doctor may recommend a breast biopsy to find out if it is cancer.
Since the area is numbed, most patients describe it as a pressure, rather than a pain, though some report pain. There can be bruising and soreness in the days after.

media.alt: Medical diagram of an ultrasound-guided breast biopsy, showing a needle inserted toward a mass in the breast while an ultrasound probe is held against the skin.

items.text: The area is cleaned and numbed with local anesthesia (this feels similar to when you go to the dentist and they use numbing gel)
sub: For lumps that can be seen with ultrasound, under ultrasound guidance, a hollow needle is inserted to remove small cores of tissue
For findings that can only be seen with mammography or contrast-enhanced mammography, under X-ray guidance a hollow needle is inserted to remove small cores of tissue
For findings only seen on breast MRI under MRI guidance a hollow needle is inserted to remove small cores of tissue.

items.text: The samples are sent to the lab to be examined under the microscope by a pathologist
The findings usually take 5-10 business days to result, but sometimes can take longer

items: Mammograms are the mainstay of breast cancer screening for early detection.
For women at high-risk for breast cancer, breast MRI should be used for supplemental screening.
For women with dense breasts, breast ultrasound or contrast-enhanced mammogram may be used for supplemental screening.
After an abnormal screening test, a biopsy may be needed to confirm whether breast cancer is present.

slides.title: At what age should average risk women start breast cancer screening?

notes: Some women may need to start breast cancer screening before age 40 based upon family history or genetic test results. Every woman should report new or concerning lumps to their doctor.

slides.title: How frequently should average risk women get breast cancer screening?

notes: Although there are inconsistent breast cancer screening guidelines, most high-risk women should get screened yearly.
Average-risk women can get screened every 1-2 years.

slides.title: Can a breast MRI replace mammograms for screening?

notes: If MRI is used, it should be in addition to, not instead of, a screening mammogram.

Although an MRI is more likely to find cancer than a mammogram, it might still miss some cancers that a mammogram would find, so doctors recommend both a breast MRI and mammograms for women at high risk.

columns.title: Average Risk Women
columns.subtitle: All of the following must be true:
items: No personal history of breast cancer or atypia on biopsy
Do not carry a high risk genetic mutation (such as BRCA1 or BRCA2)
No strong family history of breast or ovarian cancer

columns.title: High Risk Women
columns.subtitle: If any of the following are true:
items: Have a known breast cancer risk gene change based on genetic testing
Have a strong family history of breast or ovarian cancer
Have a lifetime risk of breast cancer of about 20-25% or greater
Have had a breast biopsy with atypia
Have had chest radiation for cancer treatment before age 30
Doctor's appointment every year
Screening mammogram every 1-2 years

columns.title: Under 40 years old
items: At initial visit, determine when to start screening
Screening may start 5 to 10 years before the youngest age of breast cancer diagnosis in a family member or based upon positive genetic testing in a breast cancer risk gene

columns.title: 40 years or older
items: Doctor's appointment every year
Annual screening mammogram alternating every 6 months with annual breast MRI

items.title: Insurance often covers screening tests
items.text: Many health plans cover routine mammograms at no cost to you—check with your provider to be sure.

items.title: Costs may vary for follow-up tests
items.text: If additional imaging or tests are needed, you may have out-of-pocket costs like copays or deductibles. Copays may be high for expensive studies like MRIs.

items.title: Call your insurance to confirm coverage
items.text: Ask what is covered, which facilities are in-network, and whether you need a referral.

items: Screening recommendations may vary among individuals based upon breast cancer risk.

Compared to average-risk people, those at high-risk for breast cancer may need to start screening at a younger age, more frequently, and with supplemental screening tests, such as breast MRI, in addition to mammogram.
Knowing your breast cancer risk can personalize your screening recommendations (see Module 1 on Breast Cancer Risk).

blocks.intro: Screening involves tradeoffs, and people weigh them differently. Move each slider to where you sit, then take the summary to your doctor.
blocks.disclaimer: This tool does not recommend a screening plan and does not give medical advice. It helps you put words to what matters to you so you can raise it with your doctor, who knows your risk.
blocks.summaryHeading: What to bring to your doctor
blocks.summaryIntro: Based on where you placed the sliders:

items.title: False alarms vs. missed cancer
items.left: A false alarm worries me most
framings: Being called back for a scare is what you dread most. Tell your doctor plainly, and ask exactly what the follow-up process involves and how fast you would get an answer.
A callback would weigh on you heavily. Ask how often follow-up testing turns out to be benign, and what support is available while you wait.
You would feel a false alarm more than most people. Ask what happens between an abnormal result and a final answer.
You lean slightly toward worrying about false alarms. Ask your doctor how often a callback leads to nothing.
You weigh both about equally. Ask your doctor to walk you through what a callback would mean for you, alongside what a missed finding would mean.
You lean slightly toward worrying about a missed finding. Ask whether anything in your history makes a missed finding more likely.
You would accept some extra callbacks to lower the chance of missing something. Ask which tests are most sensitive at your risk level.
You would put up with a good deal of follow-up to catch something early. Ask what additional screening would involve for you.
Not missing anything matters most to you, even with many callbacks. Tell your doctor you would rather investigate than wait, and ask what that looks like in practice.
summary: False alarms worry me far more than missing something.
False alarms worry me considerably more than missing something.
False alarms worry me more than missing something.
I lean slightly toward worrying about false alarms.
I weigh false alarms and missed findings about equally.
I lean slightly toward worrying about missing something.
Missing something worries me more than a false alarm.
Missing something worries me considerably more than a false alarm.
Missing something worries me far more than a false alarm.

items.title: Radiation exposure
framings: Radiation is a serious concern for you. Raise it first, and ask about breast ultrasound and breast MRI, which use no radiation at all.
Radiation genuinely worries you. Ask your doctor whether any part of your screening plan could use a test without radiation.
You would rather limit radiation where you reasonably can. Ask how many mammograms your plan would involve over the next ten years.
Radiation is a mild concern for you. Ask what your cumulative exposure would look like.
You are neither especially worried nor dismissive. Ask what your total exposure would look like on the schedule you are considering.
Radiation is a small factor for you. You may want to spend the conversation on which test is most accurate for you.
Radiation is a minor consideration. Focus on which test finds cancer most reliably at your risk level.
Radiation barely registers for you. Saying so lets the conversation go elsewhere.
Radiation is not something you weigh at all. That frees the conversation to focus on what matters more to you.
summary: Radiation exposure is a serious concern for me.
Radiation exposure genuinely worries me.
I would like to limit radiation where I can.
Radiation is a mild concern for me.
I have no strong feeling about radiation.
Radiation is a small factor for me.
Radiation is a minor consideration for me.
Radiation barely registers for me.
Radiation is not a concern for me.

items.title: Waiting for results
items.right: I'd rather wait longer for a thorough read
framings: The waiting is the worst part for you. Ask who will call you, exactly when, and whether results can come any sooner.
Waiting is very hard for you. Ask for the typical turnaround where you would be treated, and how you will be told.
Waiting is stressful for you. Ask what the timeline usually looks like so there are no surprises.
You would rather not wait long. Ask when you should expect to hear, and who to call if you do not.
You can tolerate the wait as long as you know what to expect. Ask for a realistic timeline up front.
You can sit with a wait if it means a careful read. Ask what the reading process involves.
You would rather the reading be unhurried. Ask whether a second read is standard, and what that adds to the timeline.
You would happily wait longer for a more careful review. Ask what a thorough read involves and who performs it.
A careful read matters far more to you than a fast one. Tell your doctor you would rather wait than have anything rushed.

Waiting for results is stressful for me.

items.title: Screening frequency
items.left: Screen me more often, even with more callbacks
items.right: Space it out, even if something's caught a bit later
framings: You want screening as often as your risk level allows. Ask what the most frequent appropriate schedule would be for you.
You lean strongly toward frequent screening. Ask whether yearly screening is recommended at your risk level.
You would prefer the shorter interval. Ask what your risk category suggests.
You lean slightly toward screening more often. Ask what the difference between the intervals means for you.
You are open to either interval. Ask your doctor which one your risk level points to, and why.
You lean slightly toward spacing screening out. Ask what the longer interval would mean at your risk level.
You would prefer the longer interval if it is reasonable for you. Ask what spacing is safe given your risk.
You would rather screen less often. Ask your doctor what the longest safe interval is for you.
You want screening spaced out as much as is safe. Ask what the longest safe interval is at your risk level, and what the tradeoff is.

items.title: Cost and access
items.left: I want the most thorough option regardless of cost
items.right: Cost and coverage matter a lot to my choice
framings: Cost is not a constraint for you. Spend the conversation on which test is most accurate at your risk level.

Cost will strongly shape what you choose. Call your insurance before scheduling to confirm coverage.
Cost and coverage will decide this for you. Call your insurance first and ask what is covered, which facilities are in network, and whether a referral is needed.
